usamts-1998-r1-01.title: Work modulo 8
usamts-1998-r1-01.body:
Subtract 90: $19m + 8n = 1908$.

Since $8n$ is a multiple of 8, $19m$ must leave the same remainder as $1908$ when divided by 8. Now $1908 = 8\cdot 238 + 4$, so $19m \equiv 4 \pmod 8$. As $19 \equiv 3 \pmod 8$, this says $3m \equiv 4 \pmod 8$. Multiplying by 3 (and $3\cdot 3 = 9 \equiv 1$) gives $m \equiv 12 \equiv 4 \pmod 8$.

So the possible values of $m$ are $4, 12, 20, \dots$ (as long as $n$ stays positive). The smallest is $m = 4$, and then
$$8n = 1908 - 76 = 1832,\qquad n = 229 > 0.$$

Check: $19\cdot 4 + 90 + 8\cdot 229 = 76 + 90 + 1832 = 1998$. ✓

**Answer: $(m, n) = (4, 229)$**

usamts-1998-r1-01.title: General solution
usamts-1998-r1-01.body:
From $19m + 8n = 1908$ and the known solution $(100, 1)$ (indeed $1900 + 8 = 1908$), every integer solution is
$$(m, n) = (100 - 8t,\ 1 + 19t)$$
for an integer $t$: if $19m + 8n = 19\cdot 100 + 8\cdot 1$ then $19(100 - m) = 8(n - 1)$, and since $\gcd(19, 8) = 1$, $8 \mid 100 - m$.

To make $m$ as small as possible while positive, take the largest $t$ with $100 - 8t > 0$, namely $t = 12$: $m = 100 - 96 = 4$, $n = 1 + 228 = 229$.

**Answer: $(4, 229)$**

usamts-1998-r1-02.title: Case analysis on the smallest denominator
usamts-1998-r1-02.body:
We need the largest possible value of $S = \frac1k + \frac1m + \frac1n$ subject to $S < 1$; the answer $\frac rs$ is this maximum (it exists because we will check finitely many cases). By symmetry assume $k \le m \le n$.

* $k = 1$ is impossible, since then $S > 1$.
* **$k \ge 4$:** then $S \le \frac14 + \frac14 + \frac14 = \frac34$.
* **$k = 3$:** then $m \ge 3$.
  * If $m = 3$, we need $\frac1n < \frac13$, so $n \ge 4$ and $S \le \frac13 + \frac13 + \frac14 = \frac{11}{12}$.
  * If $m \ge 4$, then $n \ge 4$ and $S \le \frac13 + \frac14 + \frac14 = \frac56$.
* **$k = 2$:** then $m \ge 3$ (if $m = 2$ then $S > 1$).
  * If $m = 3$, we need $\frac1n < 1 - \frac12 - \frac13 = \frac16$, so $n \ge 7$ and $S \le \frac12 + \frac13 + \frac17 = \frac{41}{42}$.
  * If $m = 4$, we need $\frac1n < \frac14$, so $n \ge 5$ and $S \le \frac12 + \frac14 + \frac15 = \frac{19}{20}$.
  * If $m \ge 5$, then $n \ge 5$ and $S \le \frac12 + \frac15 + \frac15 = \frac{9}{10}$.

Compare the bounds: $\frac{41}{42} \approx 0.976$ is larger than $\frac{19}{20} = 0.95$, $\frac{11}{12} \approx 0.917$, $\frac{9}{10}$, $\frac56$ and $\frac34$. Hence always $S \le \frac{41}{42}$, with equality for $(k, m, n) = (2, 3, 7)$. Any smaller number would fail for $(2, 3, 7)$, so the smallest valid $\frac rs$ is $\frac{41}{42}$.

**Answer: $\frac{41}{42}$**

usamts-1998-r1-03.title: Divisibility, then fill in
usamts-1998-r1-03.body:
**Which number is left out.** Let the common average be the integer $a$. Each of the 3 rows has 4 numbers, so the total $T$ of all 12 entries is $3 \cdot 4a = 12a$. Thus $T$ is a multiple of 12.

The four given entries sum to $1 + 9 + 5 + 14 = 29$ and the nine candidates sum to $77$, so if $x$ is left out, $T = 106 - x$. We need $106 - x \equiv 0 \pmod{12}$, i.e. $x \equiv 106 \equiv 10 \pmod{12}$. Among the candidates only $x = 10$ works. So **10 must be left out**, $T = 96$, $a = 8$, every row sums to $32$ and every column sums to $24$.

**Filling the array.** Label the empty cells:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline 1 & A & B & C\\\hline D & 9 & E & 5\\\hline F & G & 14 & H\\\hline\end{array}$$
The available numbers are $2, 3, 4, 7, 11, 12, 13, 15$.

* Row 2: $D + E = 32 - 14 = 18$, so $\{D, E\} = \{3, 15\}$ or $\{7, 11\}$.
* Column 1: $D + F = 24 - 1 = 23$, so $\{D, F\} = \{11, 12\}$ (no other pair of available numbers sums to 23).
* Together: $D = 11$, $E = 7$, $F = 12$.
* Column 3: $B = 24 - 7 - 14 = 3$.
* Row 3: $G + H = 32 - 12 - 14 = 6$, so $\{G, H\} = \{2, 4\}$.
* Column 2: $A + G = 24 - 9 = 15$; with the numbers left ($2, 4, 13, 15$) this forces $\{A, G\} = \{2, 13\}$, so $G = 2$, $A = 13$, $H = 4$.
* Finally $C = 15$; check row 1: $1 + 13 + 3 + 15 = 32$ and column 4: $15 + 5 + 4 = 24$. ✓

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline 1 & 13 & 3 & 15\\\hline 11 & 9 & 7 & 5\\\hline 12 & 2 & 14 & 4\\\hline\end{array}$$

All row sums are 32 (average 8) and all column sums are 24 (average 8). The argument also shows this arrangement is the only one.

**Answer: 10 is left out; the array is shown above.**

usamts-1998-r1-04.title: Two hinged rhombi (Moser spindle)
usamts-1998-r1-04.body:
**Construction.** Let $A$ be a point. Build a rhombus $ABDC$ of side 1 made of two equilateral triangles $ABC$ and $BCD$, so that $AD = \sqrt3$ (the long diagonal). Build a second rhombus $AEGF$ the same way (triangles $AEF$ and $EFG$, $AG = \sqrt3$), and rotate it about $A$ until $DG = 1$. This is possible: as the angle $\varphi = \angle DAG$ grows from $0$, the distance $DG = 2\sqrt3\sin\frac\varphi2$ grows continuously from $0$, and it equals 1 when $\sin\frac\varphi2 = \frac{1}{2\sqrt3}$ ($\varphi \approx 33.6^\circ$).

Concretely, with $A = (0,0)$: $B, C = \left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}, \pm\frac12\right)$, $D = (\sqrt3, 0)$, and $E, F, G$ the images of $B, C, D$ under rotation by $\varphi$ about $A$. The seven points are distinct (for example $E, F$ lie on the unit circle around $A$ at angles $\varphi \pm 30^\circ$, while $B, C$ are at $\pm 30^\circ$).

The unit segments are the 11 segments
$$AB, AC, BC, BD, CD,\quad AE, AF, EF, EG, FG,\quad DG.$$
(Sketch: two thin diamonds hinged at $A$, opening at a small angle, with their tips $D$ and $G$ joined by a unit segment.)

**Verification.** Suppose three of the points had no two at unit distance.

* If $A$ is one of them, the other two cannot be $B, C, E, F$ (all at distance 1 from $A$), so they must be $D$ and $G$ — but $DG = 1$. Contradiction.
* If $A$ is not among them, the three points come from $\{B, C, D\}$ and $\{E, F, G\}$. Each of these is an equilateral unit triangle, so at most one point can come from each, giving at most 2 points. Contradiction.

Hence among any three of the seven points, two are a unit distance apart. ∎

usamts-1998-r1-05.title: Cut along the lines of symmetry
Average over the symmetries
usamts-1998-r1-05.body:
Write $R_1 - R_2 + R_3 - R_4 = \iint_{\text{ellipse}} \operatorname{sgn}(x)\operatorname{sgn}(y)\,dA$, since the sign is $+1$ in quadrants I and III and $-1$ in II and IV.

The ellipse is unchanged by $x \mapsto 38 - x$ and by $y \mapsto 196 - y$ (reflections in $x = 19$ and $y = 98$). So we may replace the integrand by its average over the four images of each point:
$$\tfrac14\big(\operatorname{sgn}x + \operatorname{sgn}(38-x)\big)\big(\operatorname{sgn}y + \operatorname{sgn}(196-y)\big).$$
Now $\operatorname{sgn}x + \operatorname{sgn}(38 - x)$ equals $2$ if $0 < x < 38$ and $0$ otherwise (except on lines of zero area); similarly for $y$ with $0 < y < 196$. So the averaged integrand is $1$ on the rectangle $(0, 38)\times(0, 196)$ and $0$ elsewhere.

That rectangle lies inside the ellipse (its corners, e.g. $(0,0)$, give $19 + 98 = 117 < 1998$, and the ellipse is convex). Hence
$$R_1 - R_2 + R_3 - R_4 = 38 \cdot 196 = 7448.$$

**Answer: 7448**
